summary: The TRILL base protocol (RFC 6325) leaves minimal hooks for safely extending its header. This document specifies an initial extension that provides additional flag bits and defines some of those bits. It updates RFC 6325.

plainLanguage.summary: TRILL switches carry a header that can be extended, but the base rules never said what goes in the extension. This document defines that first word: a set of one-bit flags that tell switches about extra features, and three summary bits that let a switch drop a frame it cannot handle safely.

subtitle: Defines the first extension word of the TRILL header, so switches can carry extra flags safely.

tldr.problem: The base TRILL protocol offers hooks for extending the TRILL header, but apart from two bits it says nothing about how those extensions are laid out, so there was no safe way to add one.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines the first 32-bit word of the extension area as a set of extended header flags, with three critical summary bits at the top that let a switch decide quickly whether it can handle a frame.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from May 2014, updated by RFC 7780, and it updates RFC 6325 with the structure and the first two real flags.

today: RFC 7179 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014. It is updated by RFC 7780 and it updates RFC 6325, so the extended header flags word remains the structure for TRILL header extensions.

sections.title: What the Base Protocol Left Open
sections.content:
The base IETF Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links protocol (RFC 6325) provides a TRILL Header extension feature and describes minimal hooks to safely support header extensions, calling it "options" in Section 3.8. Apart from the first two bits, though, the base document does not specify the structure of extensions to the TRILL Header or the details of any particular extension.

This document is consistent with RFC 6325 and provides those further details. It specifies an initial extension word providing additional flag bits, and it specifies some of those bits. Additional extensions, including TLV-encoded options, may be specified in later documents. Devices implementing the TRILL protocol are called RBridges, or TRILL switches, and the terminology of RFC 6325 is used with the same meaning throughout.
sections.plainLanguage: The original TRILL rules left a gap: they allowed extra header space but never said what it would hold, so nobody could safely use it.

sections.title: The Extension Area and the Rules Around It
sections.content:
The base TRILL protocol includes a feature for extension of the TRILL Header. The 5-bit Op-Length header field gives the length of the extensions to the TRILL Header in units of 4 octets, which allows up to 124 octets of header extension. If Op-Length is zero there are no header extensions present; otherwise the extension area follows immediately after the Ingress RBridge Nickname field of the TRILL Header. The first 32-bit word of the optional extensions area consists of an extended flags area and critical summary bits.

Provision is made for several kinds of flag. Hop-by-hop flags might affect any RBridge that receives a TRILL Data frame with such a flag set. Ingress-to-egress flags would only necessarily affect the RBridge where a TRILL frame is decapsulated. Other flags may affect a class of RBridges not yet specified, for example border RBridges in a TRILL campus extended to support multi-level IS-IS. Flags may also be critical or non-critical.

Any RBridge receiving a frame with a critical hop-by-hop extension it does not implement MUST discard the frame, because it is unsafe to process a frame without understanding such an extension. Any egress RBridge receiving a frame with a critical ingress-to-egress extension it does not implement MUST drop the frame if it is a unicast frame, where the TRILL Header M bit is zero; for a multi-destination TRILL Data frame, with M equal to one, it MUST NOT be egressed at that RBridge, though the RBridge still forwards it on the distribution tree. Non-critical extensions can be safely ignored.

Any extended flag indicating a significant change in the structure or interpretation of later parts of the frame that, if the extended flag were ignored, could cause a failure of service or a violation of security policy MUST be a critical extension. If such an extended flag affects any fields that transit RBridges will examine, it MUST be a hop-by-hop critical extended flag. Most RBridge implementations are expected to be optimised for simple and common cases of frame forwarding and processing, and although the hard limit on the extension area length, the 32-bit alignment of the area and the critical summary bits are intended to help efficient hardware processing, the inclusion of extensions may cause a frame to be handled on a slow path with inferior performance, and limited slow path throughput could cause some such frames to be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: There is room for up to 124 octets of extra header. A switch that meets a flag it does not understand throws the frame away rather than guess, unless the flag was marked non-critical.

sections.title: What RBridges Must and Must Not Do
sections.content:
All RBridges MUST check whether there are any critical flags set that are necessarily applicable to their processing of the frame. To help with this, critical summary bits are provided that cover not only the extended flags specified in this document but also any further extensions that may be specified in future documents. If an RBridge does not implement all the critical flags in a TRILL Data frame, it MUST treat the frame as having an unimplemented critical extension. A transit or egress RBridge may assume that the critical summary bits are correct.

In addition, a transit RBridge MAY set or clear hop-by-hop flags as specified for such flags. It MUST adjust the length of the extensions area, including changing Op-Length in the TRILL Header, when it adds or removes the extended header flags word. It MUST correctly set the critical summary bits in the extended header flags word if it adds that word or changes any critical flags. It MUST NOT remove the extended header flags word unless it is all zero, either on arrival or after permitted modifications. And it MUST NOT set or clear ingress-to-egress or reserved extended header flags except as specifically permitted in the specification of such flags.
sections.plainLanguage: A switch that forwards a frame must keep the extension word honest: update the length field when it changes the word, keep the summary bits in step, and leave alone the flags that belong to other switches.

sections.title: No Critical Surprises
sections.content:
RBridges advertise the extended header flags they support in IS-IS protocol data units, as specified in RFC 7176. Unless an RBridge advertises support for a critical extended header flag, it will not normally receive frames with that flag set. An RBridge is not required to support any extensions at all.

An RBridge SHOULD NOT set a critical extended flag in a frame unless, for a critical hop-by-hop flag, it has determined that the next hop RBridge or RBridges that will accept the frame support that flag; for a critical ingress-to-egress flag, that the RBridge or RBridges that will egress the frame support it; or, for a critical reserved flag, that it understands which RBridges the flag applies to and has determined that those RBridges support it. SHOULD NOT is used because there may be cases where it is acceptable for those frames, particularly in the multi-destination case, to be discarded or not egressed by any RBridge that does not implement the flag.

Conflicting extensions, including extended header flags that conflict with one another, would be undesirable, because the results would be unpredictable if different implementations processed them in different orders. Rules to predictably process conflicting extensions could be defined, but they would also limit implementation flexibility and could impose substantial processing burdens. Conflicting extensions SHOULD NOT be defined, but if they are, careful thought should be given to whether and how to specify the handling of conflicting extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not set a critical flag unless you know the switches ahead of you understand it, and do not define two extensions that contradict each other.

sections.title: The Extended Header Flags Word
sections.content:
If any extensions are present in a TRILL Header, as indicated by a non-zero Op-Length field, the first 32 bits of the extensions area consist of extended header flags. The remainder of the extensions area, if any, after the initial 32 bits may be specified in later documents. Any RBridge adding an extensions area to a TRILL Header must set the first 32 bits to zero except when permitted or required to set one or more of those bits as specified. For TRILL Data frames with extensions present, any transit RBridge that does not discard the frame MUST transparently copy the extended flags word, except for modifications permitted by an extension implemented by that RBridge.

The word is laid out as follows. Bits 0 to 2 are the critical summary bits: CHbHS, CItES and CRSVS. Bits 3 to 7 are the critical hop-by-hop extended flag bits, CHbH. Bits 8 to 13 are the non-critical hop-by-hop bits, NCHbH. Bits 14 to 16 are the critical reserved bits, CRSV, and bits 17 to 20 are the non-critical reserved bits, NCRSV. Bits 21 to 26 are the critical ingress-to-egress bits, CItE, and bits 27 to 31 are the non-critical ingress-to-egress bits, NCItE.
sections.plainLanguage: The 32-bit word is split into groups: three summary bits at the top, then pairs of critical and non-critical bits for hop-by-hop, reserved and ingress-to-egress flags.

sections.title: The Three Critical Summary Bits
sections.content:
The critical summary bits summarise the presence of critical extensions. The CHbHS bit, the Critical Hop-by-Hop Summary, when set to one means one or more critical hop-by-hop extensions are present. These might be critical hop-by-hop extended header flags or critical hop-by-hop extensions after the first word in the extensions area. Transit RBridges that do not support all the critical hop-by-hop extensions present, for example an RBridge that supports no critical hop-by-hop extensions, MUST drop the frame. If the bit is zero, the frame is safe, from the point of view of extensions processing, for a transit RBridge to forward regardless of which extensions it supports.

The CItES bit, the Critical Ingress-to-Egress Summary, when set means one or more critical ingress-to-egress extensions are present, and when zero no such extensions are present. If either CHbHS or CItES is non-zero, egress RBridges that do not support all the critical extensions present MUST drop the frame. If both are zero, the frame is safe for an egress RBridge to process regardless of which extensions it supports.

The CRSVS bit, the Critical Reserved Summary, when set means one or more critical extensions are present that are reserved to apply to a class of RBridges to be specified in the future, for example border RBridges in a TRILL campus extended to support multi-level IS-IS. That class will be a subset of transit RBridges, and RBridges in the class MUST drop frames with the bit set unless they implement all the critical hop-by-hop and all the critical reserved extensions present in the frame.

The summary bits enable simple and efficient processing. An RBridge that supports no critical extensions needs only to check whether Op-Length is non-zero and, if it is, look at the top one, two or three bits just after the fixed portion of the TRILL Header, and from those decide whether to discard the frame or forward and process it.
sections.plainLanguage: Three bits at the top of the word tell a switch whether it needs to understand the rest. If they are all clear, the switch can ignore everything else in the extension area.

sections.title: The First Real Flags: Channel Alert
sections.content:
The table of extended header flag assignments shows the current state. Bits 0 to 2 are the critical summary bits. Bits 3 to 6 are available critical hop-by-hop flags. Bit 7 is the critical Channel Alert flag and bit 8 the non-critical Channel Alert flag. Bits 9 to 13 are available non-critical hop-by-hop flags, bits 14 to 16 available critical reserved flags, bits 17 to 20 available non-critical reserved flags, bits 21 to 26 available critical ingress-to-egress flags, and bits 27 to 31 available non-critical ingress-to-egress flags.

The RBridge Channel Alert extended header flags indicate that the frame is an RBridge Channel frame (RFC 7178) that requests processing at each hop. If the critical Channel Alert flag, bit 7, is one and the RBridge does not implement the RBridge Channel feature or the particular RBridge Channel protocol involved, or the frame does not actually appear to be an RBridge Channel message, then the frame is discarded. That permits, for example, a channel message requiring strict source routing, with assurance that it will be discarded rather than deviate from the directed path.

If the frame is not discarded in that way, the presence of either the critical or non-critical Channel Alert flag alerts transit RBridges to the presence of an RBridge Channel message that may require special handling. The non-critical alert flag supports, for example, an RBridge Channel protocol message with a record route function where not recording transit RBridges that do not support that function is acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: The first flags to be defined say that a frame needs handling at every hop. The critical version stops a switch that does not understand it from carrying the frame at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For general TRILL protocol security considerations the document points to RFC 6325, and for considerations related to a particular extended header flag it points to the document where that flag is specified.

It is important that the critical summary bits in the extended header flags word be set properly. If they are set when critical extensions of the appropriate category are not present, frames may be unnecessarily discarded. If they are not set when critical extensions are present, frames may be mishandled or corrupted, and intended security policies may be violated.

The RBridge Channel Alert flags have their own considerations. Implementations should keep in mind that they might be erroneously set in a frame. If either flag is found set in a frame that is not an RBridge Channel message, the flag MAY be cleared and should have no effect except, possibly, delaying processing of the frame. If either flag is erroneously omitted from a frame, the desired per-hop processing for that frame may not occur.
sections.plainLanguage: Getting the summary bits wrong is the risk: set them when nothing needs them and frames get thrown away for no reason, leave them clear when something does need them and a frame gets handled unsafely.

items.label: CRITICAL HOP-BY-HOP
items.desc: Critical hop-by-hop extensions are present. Transit switches that lack them must drop the frame.

items.label: CRITICAL INGRESS-TO-EGRESS
items.desc: Critical ingress-to-egress extensions are present. Egress switches that lack them must drop the frame.

items.label: CRITICAL RESERVED
items.desc: Critical extensions for a class of switches not yet defined. Only that class must drop the frame.
